utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said page 22, line?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Question is at page 22, line 18 and 19, and the answer begins on page 22, line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And continues to page 23, lines 1 through 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, with regard to, once again, the issue of ricochet, what you were able to determine was that there was a ricochet, but the angle of deflection was something that you were not able to determine?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. When you were taking the courses that you were taking in your military police training as a crime technician, did you take any courses or receive any information with regard to the issue of deflection angles and ricochets with regard to the -- with regard to ballistics in general and with regard to missiles in specific?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that they talked to us about that. Maybe they did, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Did you receive any on-the-job training with regard to the physics of ricochet, deflection, and trajectory?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: If I can say that this is a simple conclusion here, a simple finding between the two points of ricochet, what we assumed was ricochet, using basic human knowledge without any expertise, it is possible to establish the direction from which the shell arrived. So it's not an expert type of a finding or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And to the extent that your finding is based upon your knowledge of where you believed there to be an aggressor position, as you've defined it, that is one of the matters that weighed heavy in your determination of this conclusion; is it not?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sure. And to the extent that your finding is based upon your knowledge of where you believed there to be an aggressor position, as you've defined it, that is one of the matters that weighed heavy in your determination of this conclusion; is it not?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The direction from which the bomb or the shell arrived, whatever you want to call it, roughly determined the direction was clear, and it had nothing to do, nothing to do with where the aggressor's positions were. Such type of weapons simply had to be located in the aggressor's territory because people in Sarajevo generally knew what kind of weaponry was in the hands of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this type of machinery, if I can call it that, would have definitely been observed within the territory. When it comes to this particular shell, the finding was rather clear. One could rather clearly determine from which direction the shell had arrived, not its exact trajectory, but the direction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When you were taking the classes that you were taking on ballistics, were you trained that what people generally knew or believed to be was a basis upon which to make a determination with regard to a crime scene?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Either allow me to read the question one more time or repeat it, whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Whatever works for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Then please let me read it one more time. No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. One final matter. When you -- well, let me preface that, and I ask you this question: You seem like a gentleman with a good memory. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really think so, especially where we are talking about things that happened 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And would you take the position that your memory was better 15 years ago, obviously, than it is today, then?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean about this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: But of course it would be fresher then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of the correction that you made in your testimony concerning what you'd said previously in your statement concerning seeing an air-bomb, your statement was made in 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: That I had seen the bomb? I think my statement was given much later, when I came here in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Would it refresh your recollection if I told you that your first statement was given on the 10th of March, 1997, and at that time you were interviewed by Stephen R. Upton with the interpreter of Umihana Prguda?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the names, but I do remember giving a statement in regard to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And then you gave a second statement, correct, and that was a statement that you gave in 2006, I believe, the 25th of April, 2006?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I thought it was 2007, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm trying to get at is this so I have an understanding of something. When you gave your statement in 1997, after you gave your statement, did you have a chance to read that statement?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably, but I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay, and did you have a chance when you gave that statement to see whether or not there were any corrections that needed to be made to the statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since that is standard procedure, I assume that that's how it transpired, but I can't remember really.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And when you say it's "standard procedure," I take it you have some familiarity in the taking of witness statements by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking of statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, did you ever operate as an interpreter when you were working with the United Nations as an interpreter for the Office of the Prosecutor while they were taking statements of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I mainly worked for the police, the international police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what organisation would that have been?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The IP, IPTF as part of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And how long -- for how long a period did you do that?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I think for three and a half years, but I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That obviously shows why you are familiar with the methodologies of taking statements. With regard to your statement when you gave it in 1997, you think you probably had a chance to review it but you have no specific memory of that?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And had you had a chance to review it and you'd seen something as glaring as an error of seeing something as opposed to hearing something, that's something that you certainly would have corrected at that time; is it not?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me to give an answer that would not be strictly yes or no, I would like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, can you give me an answer yes or no and then explain yourself?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly. All I wanted to say is when I was here the last time when I gave the statement, I was not sure that I had seen the bomb. In other words, 12 to 13 years had already passed and I really can't remember, but I do remember the incident. I remember the friend I was with near the airport. He was standing guard at the military police somewhere, and I remember that we followed that bomb, but I really don't remember whether I've seen it or not. So that is why I changed my statement, but I'm sure that we heard it. But whether I saw it or not, I really can't tell. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the issue of the last time that you were here, are you referring to the last time you were here when you testified?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Because in 2006, you once again confirmed that you had seen this air-bomb being launched? Do you recall that? So you said it in 1997, and then you said it again in 2006.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that I said that we followed the flight of this bomb, but whether I ever stated that I saw it being launched, I really can't remember that I ever said anything like that. Maybe I did. But I think if that is so important, maybe it would be a good idea to call the friend who was with me then. Maybe his memory is better of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to understand that which you remember and that which you don't and that which you've told people on previous occasions because when you made this first statement in 1997, at that point you were attempting to be as truthful and accurate as you possibly could be; right?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: But of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sure. And when you made the statement again in 2006, once again, you didn't all of a sudden deviate from that position and decide that you weren't going to be truthful and accurate; correct? Once again, you were trying to be truthful and accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: That I was speaking the truth both times, that is for sure, and I never tried to lie in any of these cases. If I could not remember something in 2006, I could not really claim that I could remember because I wasn't sure, and I assumed that my memory in 1997 of this event was fresher than later on, and I really can't claim that I saw something if I can't remember it, so that's honestly how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand. Just so you're clear in 2006, and I'll refresh your recollection. See whether this refreshes your recollection as to what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: "I would like to state here that sometime at the latter part of June 1995 when I was travelling with a friend from Dobrinja to Hrasnica through the tunnel, we stopped at the entrance to the tunnel at Dobrinja. Suddenly, I saw something being launched into the air from the direction of Ilidza, and there was a terrible screaming sound as this object shot through the air." Now, that is the statement that you ultimately corrected in your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us as you sit here today with regard to memory, to your memory, what happened?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: In respect of what you've just read, I can say several things, one of those being that I was with a friend who was standing guard near the tunnel. We never went through the tunnel. I remember that. I also remember that I jumped into a ditch that was near the house because we heard the screaming sound of this bomb, and it was really scary, and that's about everything that I can remember as I sit here. I assume that my memory was better in 1997 because only a couple of years had elapsed and maybe it was more precise then, but I really cannot claim it today because I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, the way that you corrected your testimony when you testified was as follows. What you said was: "We followed the sound of the bomb, but we didn't actually see it. Similarly, you can follow an aeroplane judging by its sound, although you can't see it."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And for the Court and counsel, that's page 5177, lines 21 through 23.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So clearly, you made a determination that the information that you had given on two occasions previously was inaccurate. I'm not saying that you were trying to mislead anybody, but it was inaccurate; right?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it was inaccurate. I'm just saying that I cannot remember it now as I sit here, nor could I remember it when I gave the last statement in 2007 or 2006. I thought that it would be sort of bold to claim this at that time because at that moment I really could not remember. I could not bring it up in my memory, that image. In that sense, that's what I mean. I could not claim something that I wasn't absolutely sure was correct. I don't know; maybe in 1997 when I gave my statement I did remember it, but I cannot claim that today. This is my impression today, and this is why I made this statement and why I'm changing it now because that is the thing that I'm pretty certain of. As for the rest, I really am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as you sit here today what accounts for the marked difference in your memory from seeing something to not seeing something?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Your Honours, that's a question that's been asked in different ways on several occasions, and the answer has been given as best as it can be given on several occasions, and with respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Point taken. Point taken. Point taken. I always find memory to be fascinating, so perhaps I'm a bit off point. If I could have but a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a few questions just to clear my own mind, and I think Exhibit P500 might help. I'm not quite sure. I hope that's the correct one. Can we bring it up, please. Can you scroll down a little bit. I want to see the second paragraph. Mr. Turkovic, I just want to confirm with you that when you make the statement you made at page 22 today, lines 9 and 10, I thought it was with respect to this report. I don't know how -- are we able to help the witness to see page 22, line 10? Can you see page 22, sir?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the page number. I see the beginning of the official report, the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I think you should be able to see it now. Can you see it? At line 10 -- well, let's start at line 7. You say: "To tell you the truth, there was very little that was different except that there was no crater." And can you correct me? If you look at the whole answer that you gave there, were you then speaking about the report that was just shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This was a report compiled by an investigator. It wasn't my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you see on your screen? Do you see a report, or do you see the transcript of today's proceedings?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I see the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see the report. That's funny. I'm on e-court, and I'm seeing the transcript. Okay. On the other screen, do you see page 22?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you see line 9, starting from line 9?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you gave that answer, were you speaking about this report that you are seeing on the other screen?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: It was about -- yes, I spoke about the same incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the thing is, in the transcript you say: "... except that there was no crater." Do you see that at line 10?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But on the report, it looks like you are saying that there was a crater. Can you see the report?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I can see the report. This was the report submitted by an investigator. It wasn't my report. That's one. Secondly, I don't know what I referred -- what was referred to as "crater" here. Maybe it was the crater where the second ricochet occurred. So we could say that there was a crater there, and that's the spot where we dug later on, and the final place where the bomb landed was the house, which is where the bomb impacted and exploded, and I think there was no crater there at the final destination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the report that deals with two ricochets is P501, not P500. Can I get help here? This incident, does it also have two ricochets? Because the two ricochets you referred to were clearly relating to what has been marked as P501, the report that was brought by that counsel when he was asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But there were two reports: There was my report as the crime technician onsite and the investigator's report. That's the report we see on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the report prepared by the inspector who actually conducted the investigation, the onsite investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't do any onsite investigation?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not take part in the writing of this particular report. My report was in the crime scene technician's report from the site, and this is the inspector's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. So this report and the other report are talking about the same incident?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And your testimony is that there was no crater like you told us today?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, as I sit here, I think there was no crater at the point of impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Let me move to the next point. The next point where you talked about the two ricochets. I want to find out from you how -- I know you've told us about the methodology for finding out directions, the direction from where the shell may have come. My question to you is: Where there is a ricochet, and in particular when the ricochets are two, how do you determine the direction of the source of the shell?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, based on the points that we assumed to have been the ricochet points. As I said in my earlier evidence when I was here in another case -- testifying in another case, we assumed originally that there were two bombs, and that's how we started our onsite investigation. However, as we did not find two bombs, we came to the conclusion that there were probably two ricochets, which seemed improbable even then to us, but that was the only thing that it was pointing to. So based on these points, we estimated the direction from which the bomb had come without any precise or any accuracy when this issue is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But my question is what methodology do you use under those circumstances? Surely you don't just come there like I would come, a person without training and look and say, oh, it ricochetted, it ricochetted, therefore it must have come from this direction. You must base it on some, I don't know, your training or experience that you already have, and I just want to get an explanation if you do have a methodology that you use under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I need to say that this was a unique case of this type that we found an air-bomb that ricochetted. This is a bomb that is at least 100 kilograms heavy, so that we did not have any earlier experience with ricochets in this particular type of situation. Secondly, there were four to five policeman who were present during the onsite investigation, one of them being the anti-sabotage chief and an investigator, and then as we examined the scene together, we came to this conclusion. We concluded that it must have ricochetted because there were no traces of bursts of explosion at the first two points of impact. We only found some damage on a house, and on another spot we found these rocket motors that were dug into the ground, and we did not find the bomb itself there. So only on the basis of this did we assume that it ricochetted again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say the short answer to my question is you personally -forget about the other people that were with you - you personally had no methodology for determining the origin of the bomb? Is that your short answer?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to answer no because of these two ricochets, and that is why my answer was so lengthy, and that -- in explaining how we came to the conclusion that there were two ricochets. Based on these two spots, it could be determined where the bomb had come from, so I can't say that it was based on nothing, our opinion as to where the bomb had come, but as for my opinion being an expert opinion based on some earlier experience, well, I can't really claim that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I hear you, Mr. Turkovic, and you say your opinion as to where the bomb had come was not based on nothing, and that's what I'm asking you. What was it based on? You. Don't speak for the other people. If you say they knew better and they made the determination, you don't know how, I'll accept that, but I want to know whether you had any methodology.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't have? Okay.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, if I may just add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The assessment as to the direction of where the bomb came from -- had come from was based on the two ricochet points because that points to the trajectory from point A to point B, and this also is an indication as to where it had come from. That is my opinion, and this was the generally accepted opinion. We all agreed on that, the ones who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You then asked -- you gave an acronym IPTF. What does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] International Police Task Force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And today at page 54, lines 9 to 12, you say: "I don't know. Maybe 1997 when I gave my statement I did remember it, but I cannot claim that today. This is my impression today, and this is why I made this statement and why I am changing it now because that is the thing that I am pretty certain of." My simple question to you is, what actually is your impression today?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean in respect of this bomb?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said a few moments ago, I remember the sound produced by this bomb. I remember that I first jumped seeking shelter. My friend remained above because he allegedly -- I think he said that he had already heard the sound and he knew what it was. I remember that after this, I got out of the ditch and that we sort of observed or followed the movement of this bomb. I can't remember now. I think that this bomb that we followed did not even explode. I know that we found several unexploded bombs. I remember one particularly clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I would like to ask you one question in relation to your answer to the Defence. It is at page 48, point 3 to 10, and in line 10, you said: "When it comes to this particular shell, the finding was rather clear. One could rather clearly determine from which direction the shell had arrived, not the exact trajectory, but the direction, yes." And then in other parts of your testimony, you were saying that your methodology doesn't come from refined knowledge of ballistics or complicated trajectory points but, rather, from practical know-how, that you make inferences, very simple inferences as to from the factual situation to extract some empirical generalisations that are not of a logical complex nature but are instrumentalist to orient your conclusions. Am I correctly assessing what you do? Is that what -- did I interpret well what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I do hate to interrupt, but I'm not particularly clear about what you are saying right now except that from what I understand you're leading the witness to a particular answer, which is a bit problematic to me based upon the evidence that the witness has given thus far. I do hate to interrupt, but I'm not particularly clear with regard to the question that you're asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, my question is very simple. I am trying to distinguish between two levels of knowledge in order to understand well the position of the witness. One is a level of theoretical generalisations of complex nature, and the other are the practical conclusions of somebody who has been taught elementary systems for knowing the direction of a trajectory, and I am not leading the question, and as Judge I could ask all the questions I need to in order to clarify the situation of the witness. It's not for the counsel to lead the Judge, but the Judge could ask all the questions without any limitations in order to ascertain the truth in the knowledge of what is saying. So I do not accept, Mr. Counsel, what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, I think that you and I both wish to obtain the same result. The fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Then you cannot say that I'm leading the witness. I am just asking a simple question. I want you to retract those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that based upon the evidence that this witness has given, Your Honour, this witness has not indicated that he has been taught elementary systems for knowing a trajection -- for knowing a direction of a trajectory; and with regard to the fact that that is part and parcel of what you have included in the question that you have asked this witness, to the extent that -- and which is why I said in the first instance that I was a bit confused, to the extent that we are attempting to get a clear and concise understanding of what the witness has said, it is for that reason that I was concerned with regard to the question being asked because I found it personally -- and I mean no offence to you whatsoever, Your Honour, and I really don't. I hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: We disagree completely. My questions were oriented to distinguish two levels of knowledge, because he has asserted during his position continuously that he has no refined training, that he was just instructed in how to ascertain the direction of a projectile based on simple inference as to crater and other orientations, so this I wanted for my own knowledge to ask. I was not leading the question for your benefit. It was the benefit of me and of the Bench. So I want you to accept those points that you ask the Judge that why I was leading the question. And second, please learn that the Judge has no limitation in asking these questions, and it's done only for the fairness of the trial, beyond any interest on your position or the position of the Prosecutor, and please learn not to interrupt me with nonsense questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Once again, with all due respect, did I not mean any disrespect whatsoever, but for purposes of representing my client and for purposes of making sure that we get to the very issue that we all are concerned about here, which is, in fact, the truth, there are times when it is necessary for counsel to rise. I come from a tradition where that is allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I know about tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I come from a tradition where that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I've been a professor at a law school for many years in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm well aware of that, Your Honour. I come from a tradition where that is allowed. Once again, I say to you most sincerely, I meant no disrespect whatsoever, but I in seeing the question that you asked was confused by it and was concerned. I, too, although I am an advocate for General Perisic, I, too, am interested in obtaining the truth. That is my function among others in these proceedings, and let there be no misunderstanding about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: There is a misunderstanding on your part. It has been a misunderstanding on your part. My question was not but to assert the clearness and my own understanding of the situation, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that I misapprehended your question, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I accept your apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To the extent that I was concerned about it, I will, if I find it necessary to rise, I will rise, but at no point in time that I ever rise do I mean any disrespect to any member of the Bench. I never have in the entire 30 years that I've been practicing law, and I never will. I hold you all in great respect, and it is not my intention at all to insult you or to upset you. However, where I find that there needs be rising for purposes of dealing with my client's interests, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: The Judge in this instance acted only in the benefit of a fair trial because the Bench had to understand completely and fully the situation of every moment of this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate, Your Honour, and so did I. I was trying to do the same thing. I was not -- certainly not trying to do anything but that, and to the extent you've taken umbrage, once again, I say I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I accept your apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No insult or disrespect was intended, but the concern was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's take a break and come back at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are there any questions arising from the questions by the Bench, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Turkovic, that brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you very much for taking the time off to come and testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused, and you may stand down. Please travel well going back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon, I see you standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution does not have another witness ready to commence today. We are prepared to commence with Mr. Bell tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr.?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bell. Thank you very much. In that event, court adjourned to tomorrow afternoon, courtroom III, quarter past 2.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
